gpu_skinning_compute.problem: Skinning (applying the blended bone matrices to mesh vertices) is one of the two dominant per-character costs in an animated-character pipeline, alongside animation evaluation. Done on the CPU it costs game-thread/worker-thread time proportional to vertices x influences and forces the deformed vertex buffer to be re-uploaded to the GPU every frame; done in the vertex shader it costs GPU vertex-shader time and is paid again for every pass that draws the mesh (prepass, shadow depth, main pass, velocity). The problem this method solves is to move deformation onto the GPU once, cache the result, and let every subsequent pass of the same frame reuse the already-skinned buffers, at the price of extra VRAM and a compute pass.

implementation_variants.name: Vertex-shader skinning with a bone-matrix palette in shader constants
implementation_variants.description: The classical approach, described exactly in NVIDIA's Dawn demo: concatenated bone matrices are stored as constant parameters and four bone indices plus four bone weights are passed as vertex attributes. Dawn drives 'a mesh of more than 180,000 triangles with a skeleton of 98 bones' and uses 'four matrices per vertex'. An optimisation is accumulated-matrix skinning: build the weighted sum matrix once (16 multiplies and 12 adds) so the per-attribute cost becomes a single matrix multiply.

implementation_variants.name: Unreal GPUSkinVertexFactory (default path, fixed 4 or 8 influences)
implementation_variants.description: UE's default path 'skins positions and normals / tangents using a Vertex Shader'. Default Bone Influences mode fixes the influence count at 4 or 8 depending on platform; if a vertex uses only one bone, 'the remaining three slots are filled with zero weights and still used for skinning computation'. Bone indices and weights are bound to vertex streams, which Epic states makes the mode 'suitable for low-end hardware and platforms'.

implementation_variants.name: Compute-shader Skin Cache with pass-through rendering (UE)
implementation_variants.description: The Skin Cache 'skins positions and normals / tangents using a Compute Shader, and the results are cached in vertex buffers then passed to GPUSkinPassThroughVertexFactory - a variation of LocalVertexFactory - for rendering'. Enabled via Project Settings > Engine > Rendering > Optimizations > Support Compute Skin Cache; per-mesh override via the 'Skin Cache Usage' dropdown (Auto / Disabled / Enabled). Required for hardware ray tracing and hair strands.

implementation_variants.name: Unlimited Bone Influences mode (9-12 influences)
implementation_variants.description: UE's second vertex-factory mode for high-quality facial/cloth deformation. 'Skeletal Meshes with bone influences between 9 and 12 are rendered with the Unlimited Bone Influences path, and bone influences between 0 to 8 are rendered with the fixed 4 / 8 bone influences path.' Epic notes 'in practice the maximum number of influences is capped to 12 because of the way Skeletal Mesh source data is stored.'

implementation_variants.name: GPU deformation graphs (UE Deformer Graph, Beta)
implementation_variants.description: 'an editor that enables you to construct vertex deformation pipelines that run exclusively on the GPU'. Note the important interaction: 'the Skin Cache path isn't used when a Deformer Graph is used to drive displacement', so the two are alternatives, not complementary for the same mesh.

implementation_variants.name: Renderer-agnostic CPU sampling + engine-provided GPU skinning (ozz-animation pattern)
implementation_variants.description: Decouple the animation runtime from skinning: ozz-animation 'is an open source c++ 3d skeletal animation engine' that is 'renderer agnostic and game-engine agnostic ... focusing on performance and memory constraints with a data-oriented design' and explicitly states 'ozz does not propose an official pipeline to load meshes and materials' - you apply 'the output of the animation stage (one matrix per joint)' to your own GPU skinning. Useful when you need a custom crowd/LOD scheduler rather than the engine default.

gpu_skinning_compute.applicability_conditions: Worth doing when (a) you draw the same skinned mesh in more than one pass per frame (prepass + shadow + base pass), which is the case in any deferred or virtual-shadow-map renderer, and (b) you have dozens to hundreds of characters on screen. It is nearly free to adopt on UE5 because Support Compute Skin Cache is a project setting and r.SkinCache.Mode defaults to 1 (enabled). It is NOT worth building from scratch for a handful of heroes in a forward renderer, where a vertex-shader path with 4 influences is already close to free.
gpu_skinning_compute.limitations: The cache is bounded: 'Maximum memory for Compute Skin Cache per world (MB)' is a per-world budget and meshes are inserted 'on a first come, first serve basis'. When the cache is full the mesh silently falls back to the GPUSkinVertexFactory path, and Epic warns this creates an LOD pathology: when a mesh switches from a high (low-detail) LOD to a low (high-detail) LOD, 'Skin Cache unloads the higher LOD but then cannot accommodate the lower LOD due to heavier memory requirements'. Optional Recompute Tangents is done per Chunk and 'along the borders of two Chunks, there can be visible seams'. Bone-index width is a hard import-time decision: 8-bit supports up to 256 bones per Section, and meshes already imported before enabling 16-bit 'must be re-imported'.
gpu_skinning_compute.required_data_and_tools: A compute-capable GPU path; per-vertex bone index + weight streams (or an unlimited-influence data path); a per-world VRAM budget you can actually measure; UE provides r.SkinCache.Visualize with Overview / Memory / RayTracingLODOffset view modes and 'r.SkinCache.SkipCompilingGPUSkinVF' to cut shader permutations. On the authoring side you need a skin-weight authoring tool that respects the influence cap.

impact.cpu: low to medium reduction (removes the CPU skinning loop and the per-frame vertex upload; does NOT remove animation evaluation, which still runs on game/worker threads)
impact.gpu: medium increase (a compute pass plus recompute-tangents passes if enabled) but usually a net GPU win because shadow/prepass/main passes stop re-skinning
impact.vram: medium to high (cached skinned vertex buffers per world; the documented budget is in MB per world and overflow silently degrades quality)

gpu_skinning_compute.quality_impact: Neutral to positive. Recompute Tangents can improve normal quality after deformation but introduces Chunk-border seams; the fallback path can make quality vary frame to frame depending on cache pressure, which shows up as popping rather than as a steady frame-time cost.
gpu_skinning_compute.concept_impact: Decouples character count from CPU skinning cost and makes crowd scenes feasible; also makes GPU-driven features (hardware ray tracing, hair strands) possible at all, since Epic requires the Skin Cache for them.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1d enabling Support Compute Skin Cache + setting Default Skin Cache Behavior + 1d per-mesh Skin Cache Usage audit on hero characters + 2d sizing 'Maximum memory for Compute Skin Cache per world (MB)' against worst-case crowds + 1d deciding Recompute Tangents policy and checking Chunk seams + 1d re-import pass if 16-bit bone index is needed. p80 adds 10d for the LOD-thrash fallback investigation and unlisted off-screen/LOD regressions. This is adoption cost on UE5, NOT the cost of writing a compute skinner from scratch.

relations.note: Skin Cache removes per-vertex deformation cost; the animation budget allocator removes evaluation cost. You normally need both for crowds, because the cache does not make animation evaluation cheaper.
Smaller/faster-decompressing clips feed the evaluation stage that produces the matrices the skinner consumes; compression affects CPU, skinning affects GPU.
Retopology decisions set vertex counts and influence counts, which directly set Skin Cache VRAM occupancy and the 4/8/12-influence path a mesh takes.

Motion matching jumps between arbitrary frames, so poses can change abruptly; if the skin cache budget is exceeded the fallback path makes quality non-deterministic under exactly the conditions where motion matching is most visible.

gpu_skinning_compute.verification: Measure with GPU capture (RenderDoc/PIX) the delta in total vertex-shader invocations across prepass + shadow depth + base pass with r.SkinCache.Mode 0 vs 1; then use r.SkinCache.Visualize Memory with a worst-case crowd to confirm the per-world MB budget is never exceeded, and confirm no mesh silently falls back by watching for the LOD-switch pathology Epic describes.

claims.statement: Unreal's Skin Cache 'skins positions and normals / tangents using a Compute Shader, and the results are cached in vertex buffers then passed to GPUSkinPassThroughVertexFactory - a variation of LocalVertexFactory - for rendering'. It is enabled by 'r.SkinCache.Mode', which 'By default, it is enabled (1)'.
claims.locator: ## Skin Cache System; #### Console Commands -> r.SkinCache.Mode
claims.context: UE 5.8 PC/console.

claims.statement: Skin Cache VRAM is explicitly budgeted per world: 'Maximum memory for Compute Skin Cache per world (MB) sets the maximum amount of memory (in megabytes) per world / scene allowed for the Compute Skin Cache'. Overflow degrades silently: 'If the Skin Cache is full and cannot accommodate another Skeletal Mesh, that mesh instead goes through the GPUSkinVertexFactory path.'
claims.locator: ## Skin Cache System -> Maximum memory for Compute Skin Cache per world (MB)
claims.context: Epic publishes the knob but no recommended value; it must be sized per project.

claims.statement: Bone index width is an import-time decision with hard limits: 'An 8-bit bone index supports up to 256 bones per Section where a 16-bit bone index supports anything above 256 bones.' 'By default, all meshes are imported using an 8-bit bone index.' Meshes imported before enabling 16-bit 'must be re-imported'. Default maximum bones per Section is 65536; 'Mobile platforms have a capped maximum of 75 bones per Section.'
claims.locator: ### 8-bit and 16-bit Bone Indexes; ### Max Bones Per Section

claims.statement: Influence counts select the code path: 'Default Bone Influences mode controls whether each vertex can be skinned by either 4 or 8 influences (depending on platform support)' and 'Skeletal Meshes with bone influences between 9 and 12 are rendered with the Unlimited Bone Influences path', with 'in practice the maximum number of influences is capped to 12 because of the way Skeletal Mesh source data is stored'.
claims.locator: ## GPU Skinned Vertex Factory; ### Unlimited Bone Influence Mode
claims.context: Influence budget is an authoring constraint, not a runtime slider.

claims.statement: The reference GPU-skinning description from NVIDIA's Dawn demo: 'In the Dawn demo, we drive a mesh of more than 180,000 triangles with a skeleton of 98 bones.' 'We found that four matrices per vertex was more than enough ... so each vertex had to have four bone indices and four bone weights stored as vertex input attributes (the last two of the 16 xyzw vertex registers).' The concatenated matrices 'are stored as constant parameters'.
claims.locator: ## 4.4 Skinning; #### 4.3.2 Morph Target Implementation (16 attribute registers)
claims.context: 2004-era GeForce FX hardware; counts are structural, not a modern benchmark.

claims.statement: Accumulated-matrix skinning costs '16 multiplies and 12 adds' to build the weighted sum matrix, after which 'it now takes only a single matrix multiply to skin a point or vector'. Baseline costs given: 'multiplying a point by a matrix is implemented as four dot products and three adds, and vector-multiply is three dot products and two adds'.
claims.locator: #### 4.4.1 Accumulated Matrix Skinning
claims.context: Instruction counts on 2004 shader hardware; useful as a relative model, not as absolute cost.

claims.statement: Recompute Tangents is limited by Chunk granularity: 'each Chunk is processed independently from other Chunks of the mesh. Therefore, the vertices of a Chunk connected with adjacent Chunk(s) have no awareness of their connectivity. As a result, along the borders of two Chunks, there can be visible seams.' Default is '2 only recompute tangents on Skeletal Meshes that have enabled them on their Sections.'
claims.locator: ### Recompute Tangents -> Global Settings, and the Chunk limitation paragraph
claims.context: Seams are a visual bug class that only appears after enabling this option.

game_examples.fact: The canonical published GPU-skinning implementation: a skeleton of 98 bones driving a mesh of more than 180,000 triangles with four bone matrices per vertex, bone palette in vertex-shader constants.
game_examples.non_transferable: A single hero character on 2004 hardware, no crowd, no multi-pass reuse, no cache budget. It demonstrates the algorithm, not the economics of a modern 100-character scene.

game_examples.game: Valley of the Ancient (Epic sample project)
game_examples.fact: Epic's own GAS/animation sample is the reference project for the shipped UE5 character pipeline, i.e. the GPUSkinVertexFactory / Skin Cache paths described in the rendering-paths documentation, rather than a bespoke skinner.
game_examples.non_transferable: A sample project with one hero character says nothing about crowd-scale skin-cache VRAM pressure, which is the actual failure mode of this method.

animation_compression.problem: Raw animation data is enormous relative to its on-screen value: an uncompressed clip stores translation, rotation and scale for every bone at every sample, and the ACL project measures the Paragon set at 4276.11 MB raw. That cost is paid four times: RAM/VRAM residency, disk and patch size, streaming bandwidth, and sampling speed at runtime ('The more memory an animation clip consumes, the slower it will be to sample it and extract a character pose at runtime'). Animation compression trades a controlled, measurable error against those costs. The hard part is not the bit packing, it is the error metric: naive per-track error produces visible end-effector drift, so production codecs measure error at a virtual vertex some distance from each bone and tighten tolerance near end effectors.

implementation_variants.name: Bitwise-only quantization (keeps every key)
implementation_variants.description: UE's 'Anim Compress Bitwise Compress Only' codec 'focuses on Bitwise compression and retains all animation keys'. Format choice per track: ACF Fixed 48No W stores rotation XYZ as 16 bits each with W dropped and reconstructed; ACF Interval Fixed 32 No W stores '11-11-10 bits per component with range reduction'; ACF Float 32No W uses 'a custom float format with 6 or 7 bits for the mantissa and 3 bits for the exponent'. Best when you cannot afford key removal because root motion or notifies depend on exact timing.

implementation_variants.name: Per-track compression with adaptive error and linear key removal
implementation_variants.description: UE's 'Anim Compress Per Track Compression' 'compresses each track individually'. Three independent mechanisms: (1) resampling ('Resample Animation', 'Min Keys for Resampling'); (2) adaptive error, where 'the error threshold will be adjusted based on the height value within the skeleton' using EffectiveErrorTolerance = Max(BaseErrorTolerance / power(ParentingDivisor, Max(Height + Bias, 0) * ParentingDivisorExponent), ZeroingThreshold); (3) linear key removal with end-effector monitoring ('As keys are tested for removal, we monitor the effects all the way down to the end effectors'). 'Anim Compress Remove Linear Keys' 'Removes any keys that are unchanged from surrounding keys'; 'Anim Compress Removes Trivial Keys' 'Removes any keys where position and orientation of Assets are unchanged from surrounding keys'; 'Anim Compress Removes Every Second Key' 'Removes every second key present in the animation' with a Min Keys floor. These are last resorts and interact badly with root motion and notify density.

implementation_variants.name: ACL (Animation Compression Library) - now the UE default recommendation
implementation_variants.description: Epic: 'It is recommended to use the default Anim Compress ACL codec for most projects, which is designed to produce the most optimal results for most use cases' and 'The Anim Compress ACL codec favors as safe a compression as possible and so it is not recommended to perform much settings tuning.' ACL measures error at a 'Default Virtual Vertex Distance' of 3cm from each bone against an 'Error Threshold' of 0.01cm, with a 'Safe Virtual Vertex Distance' for socketed/end-effector bones. 'Anim Compress Custom ACL' exists but 'is provided mostly for debugging purposes' and 'decompression can often end up being a bit slower'.

implementation_variants.name: ACL Database codec - quality-as-streaming
implementation_variants.description: 'The Anim Compress ACL Database codec exposes quality based streaming ... to selectively strip the least important keyframes of your animations that can then be optionally streamed back in or out at runtime, effectively controlling quality through streaming.' Three tiers ('Highest / Medium / Low Importance Proportion') where 'All three proportion fields must sum to 1.0'. Important caveat from Epic: in a cooked build 'no data will be streamed by default. The default visual fidelity level is at its lowest.'

implementation_variants.name: Curve (morph target / animation modifier) compression
implementation_variants.description: Three codecs: 'Compress Rich Curves' with 'Max Curve Error' and 'Use Anim Sequence Sample Rate'; 'Uniform Indexable'; 'Uniformly Sampled'. ACL's curve codec 'works especially well when compressing Morph Targets if you provide a Skeletal Mesh as a reference', with 'Morph Target Position Precision' defaulting to 0.01cm.

implementation_variants.name: Unity's import-time modes (Off / Keyframe Reduction / Optimal)
implementation_variants.description: Unity exposes Anim. Compression on the clip importer; 'Off' means 'Unity doesn't reduce keyframe count on import, which leads to the highest precision animations'. Unity's error tolerances are per-curve (rotation/position/scale) rather than skeleton-height-aware, which is the main structural difference from ACL's adaptive error.

animation_compression.applicability_conditions: Always applicable if you ship more than a few minutes of animation. Adopt ACL/per-track early: compression settings are an import-time decision, and recompressing a shipped animation set late in production means re-validating every root-motion clip and every notify. If your game is driven by root motion (which motion matching requires in UE - 'Animations used in a Motion Matching setup for locomotion must contain root motion'), prefer codecs that preserve key timing on the root track and push error budget into leaf bones.
animation_compression.limitations: Error is not uniform and not intuitive. On the Paragon set ACL v2.1.0 reaches a max error of 3.9834 cm, and the report notes 'The error is unusually high and above 1 cm for 4 exotic clips' - i.e. worst-case error lives in rare clips, which is exactly what automated QA misses. Perceived fidelity and numeric error diverge: Epic states ACL frame stripping 'can result in far less destructive compression' numerically but 'the perceived fidelity loss may be higher than using Unreal Engines default frame stripping techniques' because UE strips uniformly. Higher compression levels cost build time: 'Higher levels will be slower to compress but can yield a lower memory footprint'. Sampling cost is also affected: 'The more memory an animation clip consumes, the slower it will be to sample it'.
animation_compression.required_data_and_tools: A representative clip corpus to measure against; an error metric that measures at a virtual vertex, not per track; a skeletal mesh reference for morph-target compression; build-farm time (the Paragon set takes 22m 40.51s on a Ryzen 2950X at v2.1.0); and a QA process that plays back compressed animations in game, not just in the asset editor.

impact.cpu: low decrease at runtime (smaller working set, faster sampling) but a one-off high cost at cook time (Paragon: 22m40s; CMU: 1m45s)
impact.gpu: none directly; indirect if compressed data lets more clips stay resident
impact.ram: high decrease (Paragon 4276.11 MB -> 181.25 MB, a 23.59:1 ratio)
impact.vram: low decrease (animation data is usually CPU-resident in UE; skinning consumes matrix palettes, not clips)
impact.disk: high decrease (same ratio as RAM for non-streamed data)
impact.network: high decrease for downloadable/patchable content and for streamed quality tiers

animation_compression.quality_impact: Usually invisible if the error metric is right: on the Paragon set 99.52% of samples fall below the 0.01cm threshold and the 99th-percentile error is 0.0096 cm. Quality damage comes almost entirely from bad configuration (too-large error threshold, wrong virtual vertex distance for a giant/exotic skeleton, or stripping root-motion keys).
animation_compression.concept_impact: Makes large animation libraries shippable and patchable, and enables quality-tier streaming (ACL Database) as a memory lever that does not require authoring separate LOD animations.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1d enable ACL plugin + repoint BoneCompressionSettings in BaseEngine.ini + 1d cook the whole animation set and record size/error deltas + 2d tune Error Threshold / Virtual Vertex Distance for non-human or oversized skeletons + 1d QA pass on root-motion and socketed-bone clips. p80 adds 9d for build-farm time regression triage, per-platform codec overrides, and re-authoring clips whose error is concentrated in exotic content. This assumes you adopt a shipped codec; writing your own compressor is a multi-month project and is not included.

relations.note: Motion matching stores far more animation than a state machine, so memory per clip is the binding constraint; LMM exists precisely because motion-matching memory 'scales linearly with the amount of data used'.
Both target animation memory/CPU, but at different layers: compression reduces per-clip cost, LOD/budgeting reduces how many clips get evaluated per frame. Neither substitutes for the other.

Decompression produces the matrices the skinner consumes; ACL's stated priority order is accuracy, then decompression speed, then footprint - explicitly 'Decompression speed will not be sacrificed for a smaller memory footprint'.

ACL's error is measured on a virtual vertex 3cm from each bone as a proxy for the real mesh; if the real mesh has long limbs or extreme proportions, that proxy is wrong and visible error appears where the metric reports none.

animation_compression.verification: Cook the full animation set with the candidate codec, record compressed size and max error per clip, then play back the 20 clips with the largest error in game on the actual skeleton; separately confirm that root-motion displacement over the clip is unchanged within tolerance and that notifies still land on the same frames.

claims.statement: ACL v2.1.0 on the Paragon corpus (6558 clips, 7h 00m 45.27s, 4276.11 MB raw): 'Compressed size 181.25 MB', 'Compression ratio 23.59 : 1', 'Compression time 22m 40.51s', 'Compression speed 3218.44 KB/sec', 'Max error 3.9834 cm', 'Error 99th percentile 0.0096 cm', 'Samples below error threshold 99.52 %'.

claims.context: Measured with a 0.01cm error threshold, error sampled 3cm from each bone, on every bone at every sample.

claims.statement: Compression ratio on the Paragon corpus is '23.59 : 1' for ACL v2.1.0 (vs 20.47:1 for v2.0.0 and 20.53:1 for v1.3.0).
claims.locator: '# Paragon database performance' -> '**Compression ratio**' row

claims.locator: '# Carnegie-Mellon University database performance' v2.1.0 column; '# Data and method used'
claims.context: Publicly reproducible corpus; lower max error than Paragon because the content is cleaner (Paragon has 4 exotic clips above 1cm).

claims.statement: ACL 2.1.0 median 'decompress_pose' with a cold CPU cache, forward playback, on an iPad Pro 10.5in: clip 104_30 = 0.910 us, Trooper_1 = 2.304 us, Trooper_Main = 28.837 us. Backward and random playback are equivalent (e.g. Trooper_Main 29.782 us / 29.918 us), and 'the performance is consistent regardless of the clip sample rate and the clip playback rate'.

claims.context: Mobile ARM device, not desktop x64. Desktop CMU/Matinee curves exist only as images, so no desktop figure can be quoted.

claims.statement: ACL's error model is configured in Unreal Units: default 'Error Threshold' is 0.01 cm ('A default value of 0.01cm is appropriate for cinematographic quality and most likely does not require any tuning') and default 'Virtual Vertex Distance' is 3cm ('The default value of 3cm is generally suitable for ordinary characters but large objects or exotic characters might require fine tuning'). Bones with sockets, and bones matching KeyEndEffectorsMatchNameArray substrings (hand, eye, IK, camera), use the tighter 'Safe Virtual Vertex Distance'.
claims.locator: 'Error Threshold', 'Default Virtual Vertex Distance', 'Safe Virtual Vertex Distance' property descriptions
claims.context: These two numbers are the entire quality knob; the codec is otherwise meant to be left alone.

claims.statement: UE's built-in bitwise rotation formats have exact widths: 'ACF Fixed 48No W' stores X/Y/Z 'on 16 bits each, as quantized data' with W dropped; 'ACF Interval Fixed 32 No W' stores '11-11-10 bits per component with range reduction'; 'ACF Float 32No W' uses 'a custom float format with 6 or 7 bits for the mantissa and 3 bits for the exponent'; 'ACF None ... retains all 32 floats, performing no compression'.
claims.locator: ### Bitwise Compression Format Reference
claims.context: Useful for reasoning about memory floors when key removal is unacceptable (root motion).

claims.statement: Epic explicitly warns that lower numeric error does not mean better-looking results when frame stripping: 'While the ACL will strip keyframes that contribute the least error, it may not perform as well for individual sequences when compared to compressing entire animation sets. The error may be lower, but the perceived fidelity loss may be higher than using Unreal Engines default frame stripping techniques. Unreal Engine's frame stripping tagrets a fixed frame rate, which removes keyframes in a uniform manner.'
claims.locator: Frame stripping / streaming comparison paragraph
claims.context: Directly contradicts the naive 'lower error = better' assumption; keep both behaviours available and compare perceptually.

claims.statement: Compression level trades cook time against size: 'Set the Compression level to use from the five available levels. Higher levels will be slower to compress but can yield a lower memory footprint ... Medium strikes a good balance and is suitable for production use.' Measured ACL v2.1.0 throughput was 3218.44 KB/sec on Paragon (22m 40.51s total) and 13959.52 KB/sec on CMU (1m 45s total).
claims.locator: Compression level property description; measured times from SRC-CHC-005/006
claims.context: Throughput is CPU- and setting-dependent; treat as an order-of-magnitude cook-time budget.

game_examples.fact: ACL's reference shipped-game corpus: 6558 clips / 7h 00m 45.27s / 4276.11 MB raw, compressed to 181.25 MB (23.59:1) at a max error of 3.9834 cm. The data is used for research under NDA and is not publicly available.
game_examples.non_transferable: The ratio is a property of Paragon's clip mix (including very short clips, 2 FPS clips, world-space clips and heavy scale animation). A project with mostly short looping cycles will not reproduce 23.59:1, and the 3.98cm max error is concentrated in 4 exotic clips that a different game may not have.

game_examples.game: CMU motion capture database (academic corpus, not a shipped game)
game_examples.fact: Open benchmark for the same codec: 2534 clips at 24 FPS, 9h 49m 37.58s, 1429.38 MB raw -> 65.66 MB (21.77:1), max error 0.0495 cm, 99.96% of samples below threshold.
game_examples.non_transferable: Academic mocap at 24 FPS with no game-specific authoring (no root-motion cleanup, no exotic clips). Its max error is 80x lower than Paragon's, which is a statement about the content, not about the codec.

animation_lod_budget.problem: In a crowd or battle scene the number of animated characters exceeds any sane per-frame animation budget long before it exceeds the GPU's triangle budget. Animation evaluation is fundamentally per-character and per-frame, and Unreal is explicit that the dominant cost is not the AnimGraph: 'Generally speaking, the most performance-expensive operation of an Animation Blueprint is the Event Graph logic', which is 'evaluated each Tick, with each process occurring sequentially on the Game Thread'. Animation LOD/budgeting solves this by making update frequency and update detail a function of significance (distance, screen size, gameplay importance) under a hard, measured budget, rather than letting every character tick at full rate and hoping the frame holds.

implementation_variants.name: Animation Budget Allocator (fixed ms game-thread budget, significance-driven)
implementation_variants.description: A plugin that 'constrains the computation time allotted for animation data running on specified skeletal meshes' by setting 'a fixed budget, that can be adjusted on a per-platform basis, in milliseconds of work to perform on the game thread'. When over budget it (a) 'Stop[s] ticking on individual skeletal mesh components, and favors any present Leader Pose Component', (b) 'Performs animation updates at a lower rate', (c) 'Chooses whether or not to Interpolate between updates'. Uses SkeletalMeshComponentBudgeted and Auto Calculate Significance.

implementation_variants.name: Update Rate Optimization (URO), per-component
implementation_variants.description: The older, simpler mechanism: enable 'Enable Update Rate Optimizations' on the Skeletal Mesh Component and drive it with AnimUpdateRateTick(). Epic's guidance: 'URO will prevent your animations from ticking too often ... it is recommended to target Update Rates that perform at 15Hz and under, at appropriate distances, for most characters, as well as disabling interpolation.'

implementation_variants.name: Per-LOD bone removal + bake pose
implementation_variants.description: Reduce evaluation cost by shrinking the skeleton, not just the rate: per-LOD 'Bones to Remove' array plus 'Bake Bose' ('Select a single frame of animation to bake into a pose ... useful when automatic LOD generation is removing bones for lower detail LODs but you want to retain a finer detail that has been removed'). Removed bones appear with a dot icon in the Skeleton Tree. Related reduction settings: 'Max Bone Influence', 'Enforce Bone Boundaries', 'Merge Coincident Vertices Bones'.

implementation_variants.name: Move Event Graph work to thread-safe functions + Animation Fast Path
implementation_variants.description: Attack the cost Epic identifies as largest: 'you can optimize this process by relocating Event Graph logic to Thread Safe functions that can be evaluated simultaneously on available Worker Threads', using 'Blueprint Thread Safe Update Animation' and 'Property Access'. Separately, 'Animation Fast Path provides a way to optimize variable access inside the AnimGraph update ... enables the engine to copy parameters internally rather than executing Blueprint code'. Enable 'Warn About Blueprint Usage' to catch regressions at compile time.

implementation_variants.name: Fixed bounds to avoid per-frame bounds recomputation
implementation_variants.description: 'Enable Component Use Fixed Skel Bounds, when your character does not need access to its Physics Asset ... This will skip using a Physics Asset and will instead always use the fixed bounds defined in the Skeletal Mesh. This will also skip recalculating bounding volumes for culling for every frame, increasing performance.'

animation_lod_budget.applicability_conditions: Adopt as soon as you can put more than ~20 animated characters on screen. Two hard preconditions for the parallel-update path: Epic notes 'In UAnimInstance::NeedsImmediateUpdate ... you can see all the conditions that must be met to avoid the update phase of animation running on the game thread. If root motion is required for character movement, the parallel update cannot be performed as character movement is not multi-threaded.' This matters because motion matching locomotion is root-motion driven, so a motion-matching crowd will not get the parallel-update win.
animation_lod_budget.limitations: The budget is game-thread-only and does not bound GPU skinning or render cost. Throttling changes behaviour, not just visuals: lower update rates delay notifies, delay root-motion samples and can break animation-driven hitboxes. Interpolation is a quality patch with its own cost model ('Components are only interpolated when the time budget is exceeded', and an interpolated tick is estimated at 0.75x a normal tick). Epic's own recommendation is to prefer the Budget Allocator over URO: 'Instead of using URO, it is recommended to use the Animation Budget Allocator plugin, to control the tick rate of Animation Blueprint evaluations.' Per-LOD bone removal is manual per bone and will break any animation or socket referencing the removed bones.
animation_lod_budget.required_data_and_tools: A significance function (distance, screen size, gameplay role); Unreal Insights / the 'AnimationBudgetAllocator' stat overlay under Stat > Advanced; the in-viewport debug graph via 'a.Budget.Debug.Enabled'; 'Display Debug Update Rate Optimizations' for URO; and a QA pass that checks notifies, foot-lock and hitboxes at throttled rates.

impact.cpu: high decrease on the game thread for crowds (this is the point of the feature; it converts an unbounded cost into a bounded one)
impact.gpu: none directly (animation evaluation is CPU-side); indirect if lower update rates let more characters exist
impact.ram: low decrease if combined with per-LOD bone removal

animation_lod_budget.quality_impact: Visible at distance only if tuned correctly; the system is explicitly designed to 'maximize perceived animation quality' by favouring 'the closest, most significant meshes'. Failure mode is popping or skating on characters that the significance function ranks wrongly (e.g. a distant boss, or a character that matters gameplay-wise but is off screen - note 'MaxTickedOffsreen' defaults to 4).
animation_lod_budget.concept_impact: Turns 'how many characters can we show' from an art-direction limit into a tunable budget, which is what makes crowd/battle scenes designable at all.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 1d swap meshes to SkeletalMeshComponentBudgeted + enable Auto Calculate Significance/Auto Register + 1d set a.Budget.BudgetMs per platform (Platform Scaling table) + 2d author/verify a project significance function + 2d Event Graph -> Thread Safe migration with Property Access on the hottest anim BPs + 2d QA of notify/root-motion behaviour at throttled rates. p80 adds 12d for modular-character Leader Pose integration, off-screen tick policy, and fixing gameplay systems that assumed per-frame animation.

relations.note: Budgeting bounds game-thread evaluation cost; the skin cache bounds GPU deformation cost. Crowds need both - budgeting alone still leaves you paying skinning for every visible character.

Motion matching searches the database on tick; throttling the tick rate throttles responsiveness, and root-motion locomotion blocks the parallel-update path entirely, which removes one of the two ways to pay for motion matching in a crowd.
Compression lowers the per-character evaluation cost (smaller working set, faster sampling), which directly raises how many characters fit inside a fixed budget.

Abilities that drive montages or read animation state on tick inherit the throttled rate; a throttled character can activate an ability whose montage callback is delayed, which is a gameplay bug, not a visual one.

animation_lod_budget.verification: Run a worst-case crowd, enable the AnimationBudgetAllocator stat overlay and the a.Budget.Debug graph, and confirm the solid performance line tracks the dotted budget line instead of exceeding it; then repeat with Stat > Advanced > AnimationBudgetAllocator and confirm 'Interpolated' and 'Throttled' counts are what your significance policy predicts, and that no gameplay-important character is being interpolated.

claims.statement: The budget is expressed in milliseconds of game-thread time: 'a.Budget.BudgetMs' - 'The time in milliseconds that we allocate for Skeletal Mesh work to be performed', 'Values > 0.1, Default = 1.0'. Epic ships a platform-scaling table: [ViewDistanceQuality@0] a.Budget.BudgetMs=1.0, @1 = 1.5, @2 = 2.0, @3 = 2.5.

claims.context: 1.0 ms is the default, not a recommendation; it must be re-derived per project from the frame budget.

claims.statement: The allocator's initial cost model assumes 'a.Budget.InitialEstimatedWorkUnitTime' - 'The time in milliseconds we expect, on average, for a Skeletal Mesh component to execute', 'Default = 0.08'. 'The value only applies for the first tick of a component, after which we use the real time the tick takes.'
claims.locator: ## Additional Console Commands -> a.Budget.InitialEstimatedWorkUnitTime
claims.context: A seed value only; it is replaced by measured time after the first tick, so it affects the first frames after spawn.

claims.statement: Throttle limits are bounded by defaults: 'a.Budget.MaxTickRate' 'Default = 10' ('The maximum tick rate we allow. If this is set then we can potentially go over budget but keep the quality of individual meshes to a reasonable level'), 'a.Budget.InterpolationMaxRate' 'Default = 6', 'a.Budget.MaxInterpolatedComponents' 'Default = 16', 'a.Budget.MaxTickedOffsreen' 'Default = 4' ('The maximum number of off screen components we tick (most significant first)').

claims.context: MaxTickRate 10 means a character may update only every 10th frame at worst, i.e. 6 Hz at 60fps.

claims.statement: Epic's URO guidance gives an explicit target rate: 'it is recommended to target Update Rates that perform at 15Hz and under, at appropriate distances, for most characters, as well as disabling interpolation'. For interpolated ticks the allocator assumes an amortised cost of 'a.Budget.InterpolationTickMultiplier' 'Default = 0.75' - 'the expected value an amortized interpolated tick will take compared to a normal tick'.
claims.locator: ## General Tips -> Update Rate Optimizations bullet; SRC-CHC-001 InterpolationTickMultiplier
claims.context: 15 Hz = update every 4th frame at 60fps. Note Epic recommends the Budget Allocator instead of URO.

claims.statement: Epic states the hierarchy explicitly: 'Instead of using URO, it is recommended to use the Animation Budget Allocator plugin, to control the tick rate of Animation Blueprint evaluations.'
claims.locator: ## General Tips -> Update Rate Optimizations bullet, second paragraph
claims.context: Keep both sources: URO is still the fallback for projects that cannot take the plugin dependency.

claims.statement: Parallel animation update is blocked by root motion: 'In UAnimInstance::NeedsImmediateUpdate struct, you can see all the conditions that must be met to avoid the update phase of animation running on the game thread. If root motion is required for character movement, the parallel update cannot be performed as character movement is not multi-threaded.'
claims.locator: ## General Tips -> first bullet (conditions for Parallel Updates)
claims.context: Directly limits how much a root-motion locomotion system (including motion matching) can benefit from worker threads.

claims.statement: Skeletal LODs can also cut bones, not just triangles: 'When working with Skeletal Mesh LODs there may be situations where you want to reduce the amount of Bones in a Skeletal Mesh's Skeleton Asset alongside the reduction in the Mesh ... Within the desired LOD's LOD Info properties, navigate to the Bones to Remove property.' Removed bones 'will still be visible in the Skeleton Tree of the LOD, however they will be indicated with a dot icon rather than the usual bone icon.'
claims.locator: ## Reducing Bones
claims.context: Complementary to tick-rate throttling: fewer bones per evaluation, on top of fewer evaluations.

claims.statement: The allocator is explicitly quality-aware by design: 'It will favor the closest, most significant meshes, running their animations at the highest framerate it can while reducing the framerate and quality of less significant meshes.' Per-mesh debug labels report the update rate numerically plus Lo (low detail), Hi (high detail) and I (interpolating).
claims.locator: ## Using the Animation Budget Allocator
claims.context: Correctness therefore depends entirely on your significance function being right.

game_examples.fact: Epic's own documentation uses Fortnite's modular characters as the motivating case: characters are 'comprised of several Skeletal Meshes (heads, bodies, backpacks, etc.) all of which can be ticking at a given time', and the budgeter shows per-mesh rate numbers plus Hi/Lo/I labels. The stat overlay explicitly reports 'Num Registered Components ... including the multiple skeletal mesh components that comprise [modular characters]'.

A monolithic-mesh character project has a much smaller per-character component count and may not need the allocator at the same crowd size. Epic publishes no ms budget or character count for Fortnite, so nothing about their scale transfers.

game_examples.locator: ## Using Multi-Threaded Animation Updates -> closing paragraph
game_examples.non_transferable: Lyra is a small-scale sample; it demonstrates the migration technique, not the crowd budget that makes it necessary.

motion_matching.problem: State machines and blendspaces require an author to enumerate every transition (start, stop, pivot, turn-180) and hand-author blending between them; the combinatorial explosion is unmanageable for responsive locomotion, and every gameplay change forces an animation-graph change. Motion matching replaces authored transitions with a search: at (or near) every frame, score every frame of a large animation database against the character's current pose/velocity and against the desired future trajectory, then jump to the best match. The problem it solves is authoring scalability and responsiveness, not performance - the original description calls it 'A ridiculously brute-force approach to animation selection'.

implementation_variants.name: Brute-force full-database search
implementation_variants.description: The original formulation: 'Algorithm: Every frame, look at all mocap and jump at the best place.' Cost is O(database frames) per query, which is why Clavet's deck lists 'Optimizations (subject of a future talk): LOD, KD-Tree, Motion Shaders, Etc.' 'Trick 1: Posematch only a few bones'. 'Precompute and save with the animation for fast cost computation: Pose/Velocity Matching - Local velocity, Feet positions, Feet velocities, Weapon position'. The precomputation is what makes the brute-force search affordable.

implementation_variants.name: Trajectory matching against a predicted future
implementation_variants.description: 'Trick 2: Just check where a piece of animation brings you if you play it.' Cost terms are 'Future position, Future orientation, Future velocity/acceleration'. Critically, the prediction is game simulation, not animation: 'Run actual simulation code to predict future trajectory. Predict stops on walls and ledges', with a 'Spring damper on velocity: predictable and comfortable'. The hybrid that avoids foot sliding: 'The code decides the real simulation point'; 'Choose animations that follow the simulation. And do Displacement from Animation.' 'Animation moves and rotates the entity.' Then 'Clamp the entity 15 cm around the simulation'.

implementation_variants.name: UE Pose Search: schema channels + database + acceleration structure
implementation_variants.description: A 'Pose Search Schema' defines query channels (Trajectory, Pose, Heading, Phase, Position, Velocity, Sampling Time, Padding, plus experimental Crashing Legs / Permutation Time). A 'Pose Search Database' holds the animation. Search modes include PCAKDTree ('Number Of Principal Components' sets KDTree dimensionality) and VPTree, with 'KNNQuerryNumNeighbors' controlling how many candidates get full cost evaluation. 'Pose Pruning Similarity Threshold' saves memory by storing similar poses once.

implementation_variants.name: Normalization Sets + chooser to swap databases at runtime
implementation_variants.description: 'Pose Search Normalization Sets are a series of defined Pose Search Database assets that each contain groups of Animations that are applicable to specific use cases ... Pose Search Normalization Sets can be dynamically swapped in when specific gameplay events are triggered ... use a chooser system to dynamically set which Database is active at runtime.' This is how you stop one database from being everything.

implementation_variants.name: Learned Motion Matching (neural, no animation data in memory)
implementation_variants.description: Replace each step of the algorithm with a trained network: 'training three specialized neural networks to replace three specific components of the Motion Matching algorithm ... which does not rely on keeping any animation data in memory'. The paper's abstract: 'Our final model has no need to store animation data or additional matching meta-data in memory, meaning it scales as well as existing generative models. At the same time, we preserve the behavior of Motion Matching, retaining the quality, control, and quick iteration time which are so important in the industry.'

implementation_variants.name: Motion graphs (the predecessor, still a valid alternative)
implementation_variants.description: 'Motion Graphs - Unstructured list of animations. Preprocess: Figure out when you can jump to somewhere else', then 'When reaching a transition point, decide where to go from a list of possibilities'. Requires a dense graph for comfortable control: 'For comfortable control, we need a dense graph'.

motion_matching.applicability_conditions: Only for animation sets that are (a) mocap-derived or at least densely sampled, (b) large enough that authoring transitions is the bottleneck, and (c) driven by a predictable movement model you can simulate forward. Two hard UE preconditions: 'Animations used in a Motion Matching setup for locomotion must contain root motion, and the Animation Sequences must have the Root Motion property enabled' - and root motion is precisely what blocks parallel animation update (SRC-CHC-002). It is the wrong tool for a game with a handful of authored, non-locomotion clips, and the wrong tool if your movement model is not predictable (Epic: 'if your movement model is moving at 5 meters a second, but your data is averaged around 4 meters a second, this could result in a Motion Matching system that consistently chooses the maximum value animation poses').
motion_matching.limitations: Memory and search cost scale with the database; Epic gives only qualitative guidance ('the more channels and samples within the channels you have, the more performance it will take to run'; 'The higher the Sample Rate the more refined animation pose searches will be, but will increase the memory cost of the system'). More data is not automatically better: 'It is recommended that you use as few samples as possible. While more samples can provide the Motion Matching node with more accurate data, it can distort the system's results.' Because it jumps frames, it fights authored notifies (hence 'Should Filter Notifies' + 'Notify Recency Time Out' default 0.2s) and it fights authored timing (hence 'Pose Jump Threshold Time' and 'Pose Reselect History'). Sliding is a first-class problem, addressed by 'Lock the toe when it doesn't move too much in the main animation' and by timescaling: 'Timescale the animation according to error ratio - Predicted Error', with the counter-intuitive advice 'Just sliding often gives better results'.
motion_matching.required_data_and_tools: A large, consistently captured and marked-up mocap library; a forward-simulatable movement model (spring-damper on velocity is what Clavet used); a trajectory prediction that can predict 'stops on walls and ledges'; animation warping (slope warping, orientation correction, spine pitch bending); and a debugging harness - UE ships '## Motion Matching Debugging' and Clavet's pipeline assumes you can 'play the game without animation! (just debug display)'.

impact.cpu: medium to high increase per character (database search per query) - Epic and Clavet publish no ms figure; treat as unquantified until measured
impact.gpu: none directly (pose selection is CPU-side); indirect via higher animation fidelity
impact.ram: high increase (database scales with clip count x sample rate x channel count); LMM is the documented escape hatch
impact.disk: medium increase (far more mocap is retained than a state machine would ship)

motion_matching.quality_impact: High, when the data is there: transitions are found rather than authored, so 'Elegantly find transitions when they exist'. The same property makes it fail loudly when data is missing - there is no authored fallback to hide a gap.
motion_matching.concept_impact: Inverts the animation pipeline: instead of 'design the graph, then capture what it needs', it is 'capture broadly, then let the query find it'. This changes what animators and anim programmers do day to day, and it is the reason Fortnite-era and Ubisoft-era locomotion feels different from 2010-era locomotion.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 10d capture/clean/mark-up a locomotion mocap set with root motion + 5d schema + database authoring on UE Pose Search + 8d movement model + trajectory prediction (spring damper, wall/ledge stop prediction) + 8d blend/jump-threshold/notify-filter tuning + 6d animation warping (slope, orientation, spine pitch) + 8d tooling and debugging harness. p80 adds 50d for building the capture pipeline if you do not already have mocap, for distance/culling integration with the animation budget allocator, and for the sliding/toe-lock polish pass. This is one of the largest single-line items in this pack.

relations.note: Motion matching ships an order of magnitude more animation than a state machine; without compression the database is unshippable, and LMM exists because 'the memory usage of such methods generally scales linearly with the amount of data used'.

Root motion is mandatory for UE motion matching but also blocks parallel animation update, removing the main thread-scaling lever; you are left with tick-rate throttling, which throttles responsiveness.

Motion matching produces higher-fidelity, higher-frequency pose changes; if the skin cache is over budget, the fallback path makes quality vary with cache pressure exactly when poses are changing fastest.
A tag-driven ability system can swap Pose Search Normalization Sets on gameplay events (e.g. combat vs exploration databases), which is the natural integration point between the two systems.
Both are 'capture more than you need, then reduce' pipelines; they differ in that one reduces geometry/texture offline and the other reduces animation at query time.

motion_matching.verification: Two independent checks. (1) Data-coverage check: drive the character along a scripted path covering starts, stops, pivots at every angle and slopes, and confirm the selected clip changes are continuous (no repeated re-selection of the same short segment) and that foot sliding stays inside your tolerance. (2) Cost check: measure game-thread animation time per character with the database at 25%, 50% and 100% size to confirm the search cost model before you commit to a database size.

This means the system will be influenced three times as much about differences in trajectory than it will about differences in the pose.'

Default window: 'The default value of 0.2 can be used as a baseline as it was designed to be the most useful for biped locomotion'.

If this property is 0 then the blend stack will be disabled.' 'Store Blended Pose - When enabled, and the number of requested blends is higher than the value set for the Max Active Blends property, the blend stack will blend and accumulate into a stored pose ... When disabled, the memory to store the pose will be saved, but ... the blendstack will start discarding animations, potentially resulting in animation popping.'

The proposed fix: 'Our final model has no need to store animation data or additional matching meta-data in memory.'

game_examples.engine: Ubisoft in-house (AnvilNext-derived pipeline; animation system custom)
game_examples.fact: Motion matching was presented by Ubisoft Montreal's Simon Clavet at GDC 2016 as the studio's next-gen animation approach. The published pipeline is: 'Mocap is tweaked, imported, and marked up'; 'At runtime Gameplay makes a request (desired trajectory and event constraints)'; 'The animation system continuously finds the best piece of data to play'; 'We modify the result to precisely match gameplay and environment' - the last step being procedural warping (orientation correction, timescaling, toe locking for sliding prevention, slope warping, spine pitch bending).
game_examples.non_transferable: The talk publishes no database size, no search time, and no CPU budget - the optimisation slide explicitly defers to 'a future talk'. Also, this is a melee-combat game where weapon position and stance matching matter; a shooter or a third-person action-adventure will weight channels completely differently and cannot reuse the weighting.

normal_bake_retopology_pipeline.problem: High-detail sculpts, CAD or scanned meshes cannot ship: their triangle counts defeat LODs, skinning and shadow passes, and their UVs are usually unusable. The bake/retopology pipeline solves this by producing a low-polygon, animation-safe mesh whose UVs are authored for texturing, and by transferring the high-poly surface detail into textures (principally a tangent-space normal map, plus AO/curvature/height). Almost every visual defect in this pipeline comes from a mismatch between the assumptions of the baker and the assumptions of the renderer - most notoriously the tangent basis.

implementation_variants.name: Cage-based 'selected to active' ray-cast baking
implementation_variants.description: The standard mechanism: 'Bake shading on the surface of selected objects to the active object. The rays are cast from the low-poly object inwards towards the high-poly object.' A cage is 'a ballooned-out version of the low-poly mesh created either automatically (by adjusting the ray distance) or manually (by specifying an object to use)', configured via 'Cage Extrusion'.

implementation_variants.name: Ray-distance baking without a cage
implementation_variants.description: Simpler alternative: 'When not using a cage the rays will conform to the mesh normals. This produces glitches on the edges, but it is a preferable method when baking into planes to avoid the need of adding extra loops around the edges.' Controlled by 'Max Ray Distance - Distance to use for the inward ray cast when using Selected to Active. Ray distance is only available when not using Cage.'

implementation_variants.name: Bake directly from a multiresolution/sculpt modifier
implementation_variants.description: 'Bakes a Normal or Displacement map directly from a mesh that has a Multiresolution Modifier. This method compares two resolution levels of the modifier: Viewport Levels used as the low-resolution base mesh, Render Levels used as the high-resolution detailed mesh.' Avoids maintaining two separate objects entirely.

implementation_variants.name: A shared tangent-space standard between baker and renderer
implementation_variants.description: MikkTSpace exists precisely because the baker and the renderer must agree: 'A common standard for tangent space used in baking tools to produce normal maps.' Without it, a normal map baked in one tool shows shading seams and inverted green channels in another engine.

implementation_variants.name: Margin/gutter generation around UV islands
implementation_variants.description: 'When baking to images, by default a margin is generated around UV islands. This is important to avoid discontinuities at UV seams, due to texture filtering and mip-mapping.' Two strategies: 'Extend: Extend border pixels outwards' and 'Adjacent Faces: Fill margin using pixels from adjacent faces across UV seams.' Size is set in pixels.

implementation_variants.name: Space and swizzle matching
implementation_variants.description: 'Normals can be baked in different spaces: ... Tangent: Normals in tangent space coordinates, independent of object transformation and deformation. This is the default, and the right choice in most cases, since then the normal map can be used for animated objects too.' Object space is 'independent of object transformation, but dependent on deformation'. Blender also warns the bake-time setting 'should match the setting used for baking' in the image texture options, and exposes 'Swizzle R, G, B'.

normal_bake_retopology_pipeline.applicability_conditions: Any time you author detail above what can ship. It is mandatory for characters and hero props in a PBR pipeline. It is largely unnecessary - and actively counterproductive - for flat/vector-art pipelines where the art direction is 2D (see the relation to art_direction_stylization), because there is no high-poly source of truth to project from.
normal_bake_retopology_pipeline.limitations: Cage baking has a hard constraint on topology matching: 'Both meshes need to have the same Topology (number of faces and face order)' for a custom cage. Hard splits are a documented trap: 'Hard splits (e.g. when the Edge Split Modifier is applied) should be avoided because they will lead to non-smooth normals around the edges.' Memory is a real failure mode: 'There is a CPU fixed memory footprint for every object used to bake from. In order to avoid crashes due to lack of memory, the high-poly objects can be joined before the baking process.' And the whole pipeline silently depends on the tangent basis matching (SRC-CHC-018).
normal_bake_retopology_pipeline.required_data_and_tools: A high-poly source, a retopologised low-poly with non-overlapping UVs, a baker (Blender/Cycles, Substance, Marmoset, xNormal), a shared tangent-space implementation (MikkTSpace), and a DCC-side QA step that inspects the bake at multiple mip levels (which is where seam and margin bugs appear).

impact.cpu: none at runtime; high one-off cost at bake time (Cycles uses render settings: 'Cycles uses the render settings (samples, bounces, ...) for baking')
impact.gpu: medium decrease at runtime (fewer triangles, cheaper skinning, cheaper shadow and prepass passes)
impact.vram: low increase (normal/AO/height textures) but a large net VRAM win versus shipping the high-poly geometry

normal_bake_retopology_pipeline.quality_impact: Determines whether a character reads as the concept at close range. Bake artefacts (ray-miss mush, cage projection errors, hard-split seams, mip-level seam bleeding) are among the most common and most expensive-to-fix-late visual bugs in production.
normal_bake_retopology_pipeline.concept_impact: Enables 'sculpt at film detail, ship at game budget' - it is the pipeline that makes modern character fidelity possible, and it is also the pipeline that sets your LOD and influence budgets.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2d define the bake spec (resolution, margin, tangent space, swizzle, map set) + 3d retopology per hero character + 2d UV + 2d bake and iterate on cage/ray distance + 1d QA at multiple mip levels and in-engine. p80 adds 14d for fixing hard-split/mesh-normal issues, re-baking after late sculpt changes, and building a batch bake farm. Per hero asset; not including the art time to make the high-poly.

relations.note: Retopology sets the vertex count and the influence count, which select the 4/8/12-influence path and set Skin Cache VRAM occupancy per character.

ACL measures error at a virtual vertex 3cm from each bone as a stand-in for the real mesh; extreme retopologised proportions invalidate that proxy and produce visible error where the metric reports none.
A flat/vector art direction can skip high-to-low baking entirely; choosing stylization early removes this whole pipeline rather than optimising it.
Baked map sets are the dominant texture memory in a PBR character pipeline, so the texture-compression choice determines whether the bake detail survives to the screen.

normal_bake_retopology_pipeline.verification: Compare the low-poly with the bake applied against the high-poly from a fixed camera at hero distance and at 2x/4x distance (mip levels); check for ray-miss grey areas, cage over-projection at concave regions, and seam lines at UV island borders; then confirm the normal map's green channel orientation and tangent basis in the target engine before authoring any content on top of it.

claims.statement: Cage vs ray-distance is the central mechanical choice: 'Bake shading on the surface of selected objects to the active object. The rays are cast from the low-poly object inwards towards the high-poly object. If the high-poly object is not entirely involved by the low-poly object, you can tweak the rays start point with Max Ray Distance or Extrusion (depending on whether or not you are using cage).'

claims.statement: Cage-less baking has a documented failure mode and a documented exception where it is preferable: 'When not using a cage the rays will conform to the mesh normals. This produces glitches on the edges, but it is a preferable method when baking into planes to avoid the need of adding extra loops around the edges.'

Hard splits (e.g. when the Edge Split Modifier is applied) should be avoided because they will lead to non-smooth normals around the edges.' A custom cage also requires topology parity: 'Both meshes need to have the same Topology (number of faces and face order).'

This is important to avoid discontinuities at UV seams, due to texture filtering and mip-mapping.' This is the default, and the right choice in most cases, since then the normal map can be used for animated objects too.' It does NOT confirm any deformation, bake or streaming technique, and a 2D/vector art pipeline is not evidence about a PBR character pipeline - it is evidence that one class of project can delete this pipeline entirely.

art_direction_stylization.problem: Art direction is usually treated as a document; the engineering problem is that a stylized look is a set of non-negotiable constraints on the renderer, the asset pipeline and the animation system, and those constraints are cheap to state early and brutally expensive to retrofit. The problem this method solves is to convert an art style into an explicit, testable technical specification - which shading model, which lighting model, which silhouette and readability rules - and then to let those constraints delete work from the pipeline (PBR material variety, high-to-low bakes, per-asset lighting authoring) instead of adding to it.

implementation_variants.name: Art-direction-driven NPR shading (Team Fortress 2 model)
implementation_variants.description: Valve's paper is explicit that art and tech were designed together: 'Grounded in the conventions of early 20th century commercial illustration with 1960s industrial design elements, the look of Team Fortress 2 is the result of close collaboration between artists and engineers.' The techniques serve a gameplay requirement, not a decorative one: 'the shading techniques are designed to quickly convey geometric information in our desired illustrative style using variation in luminance and hue, so that game players are consistently able to visually read the scene.'

implementation_variants.name: Deferred toon renderer built from custom passes
implementation_variants.description: Hi-Fi RUSH: 'a stylish 3D toon art style using a customized Unreal Engine 4 ... Learn about the development of a deferred toon renderer developed for toon shading a 3D world in a 2D way. Various customized UE4 render passes along with added render passes of their own are stylized and combined inside deferred rendered post process volumes.' Discussed subsystems: 'Comic shaders, toon lights, dynamic shadow map strategies, static shadow maps, light probe GI, and their face shadow implementation'.

implementation_variants.name: Style as a hard frame-rate and resolution constraint
implementation_variants.description: Treat the target as part of the art spec, not as an optimisation afterthought. Hi-Fi RUSH is described as 'a 60fps rhythm action game rendered in a stylish 3D toon art style', with 'toon shading for the entire world, both character and environment, while providing modern 3D graphics features, all at 60fps at native resolution'. Native resolution means the style has to survive without an upscaler hiding the edges.

implementation_variants.name: 2D/vector art pipeline (delete the PBR pipeline entirely)
implementation_variants.description: UbiArt (Rayman Legends) is documented as 'an engine originally developed for the game's predecessor, Rayman Origins' whose value was iteration: 'The engine's role in improving prototyping and level design pre-production processes will be demonstrated through case studies.' Choosing a 2D art direction removes high-to-low bakes, material-authoring variety and PBR calibration from the critical path.

implementation_variants.name: Style constraints enforced as asset rules
implementation_variants.description: General practice (supported by the asset-conditioning framing in Game Engine Architecture, 'tools pipelines and the game asset database'): encode the style bible as validated importer rules - palette quantization, maximum material count, forced outline/normal conventions - so drift is a build error rather than a review comment.

art_direction_stylization.applicability_conditions: Decide at concept. Stylization is one of the few decisions that reduces total work, but only if it is made before the asset pipeline is built: a toon renderer retrofit means re-authoring lighting, materials and post for every existing scene. It is the right call when your team is art-limited rather than engineering-limited, and when the game's readability requirements (identifying characters at a glance, reading silhouettes through clutter) dominate over material realism.
art_direction_stylization.limitations: The evidence base is case studies, not measurements - no source in this pack publishes a cost or a saving for stylization, so any 'stylized is cheaper' claim is an argument, not a measurement. Stylization also removes tools: a toon renderer cannot use off-the-shelf PBR content, so middleware asset libraries and outsourced PBR art become unusable. And a style that hides detail also hides bugs (LOD popping, animation error, bake artefacts), which can defer defects to late QA.
art_direction_stylization.required_data_and_tools: A style bible that states rendering-relevant rules, not just mood; a prototype shader set; a reference board rendered in-engine rather than in 2D; and engine-side enforcement (importer validation, material templates).

impact.cpu: unknown (no source in this pack quantifies it) - stylized pipelines often drop features (fewer lights, no GI) so CPU can fall, but this is not measured
impact.gpu: unknown; a deferred toon renderer adds custom passes (Hi-Fi RUSH) but may delete expensive PBR/GI passes
impact.vram: low to medium decrease (fewer unique materials, smaller map sets; no high-to-low bake set for a 2D pipeline)
impact.disk: medium decrease for 2D/vector pipelines; roughly neutral for 3D toon

art_direction_stylization.quality_impact: Defines quality. The important engineering consequence is that 'photorealism' stops being the quality target, so QA can stop chasing PBR correctness and start chasing readability and silhouette consistency.
art_direction_stylization.concept_impact: Largest conceptual lever in this pack: it decides which of the other twelve methods you even need. A 2D/vector direction can delete normal baking and most of the character-skinning budget; a stylized 3D direction changes the shadow, VFX and ability-feedback budget substantially.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 5d style bible translated into rendering rules + 8d prototype shader set (toon/illustrative lighting + outline + face/character shadow strategy) + 5d reference scene built and reviewed in-engine + 4d importer validation rules + 3d VFX/ability-feedback language. p80 adds 35d when the decision lands after assets exist and lighting/materials must be re-authored. This is explicitly a planning estimate: no source in this pack publishes measured effort for stylization.

relations.note: A 2D/vector art direction removes the need for high-to-low bakes; a stylized 3D direction usually keeps them but changes which channels matter (curvature/AO for line work rather than micro-detail).
The VFX language is part of the style; a stylized game usually needs fewer, larger, more readable effects, which directly changes the particle/instance budget rather than just the look.
2D/vector and frame-by-frame styles put extreme pressure on sprite memory and atlas packing instead of on geometry and materials.
Flat-colour and hard-edged stylized art is exactly the content that block-compression artefacts damage most; compression choice is an art-direction decision in a 2D game.

art_direction_stylization.verification: Build one representative scene and one representative character to final quality early, and test the readability claims the style asserts: can players identify characters at maximum clutter and worst-case lighting? Then lock the spec as importer validation rules and measure the frame cost of the custom passes before content production scales.

game_examples.fact: A fully hand-drawn style executed as an asset pipeline problem: '50,000 frames of amazing hand-drawn animation', drawn and inked on paper and coloured in Photoshop, authored at '24 frames-per-second' while 'the game runs at a sparkling 60 frames-per-second'. Unity's Sprite Renderer, Sprite Packer and 2D Physics are named as the toolchain.

skeletal_2d_deform.problem: Frame-by-frame 2D animation does not scale: every new motion is new art, and blending between motions is impossible. 2D skeletal deformation solves this by attaching a bone hierarchy to a textured mesh and deforming that mesh at runtime, so motion becomes reusable data (bone transforms) instead of new pixels. The cost model is completely different from 3D skinning: the transform work is on the CPU, per vertex, per influencing bone, and the mesh is re-uploaded every frame, so the budget is measured in 'vertex transforms', not in shader instructions.

implementation_variants.name: Weighted mesh attachments (Spine model)
implementation_variants.description: 'A mesh attachment is a polygon that is textured with an image. A polygon is defined inside the image, then its vertices can be manipulated to bend and deform the image.' 'Meshes can be deformed automatically when bones are transformed by using weights.' 'Most or all deformation should be done using weights. Using deform keys should be avoided or kept to a minimum.'

implementation_variants.name: Vertex-count and influence budgeting
implementation_variants.description: The cost arithmetic is published and simple: 'Generally the number of vertices in a mesh should be kept to a minimum to reduce CPU usage. The position of each vertex must be computed by the CPU each frame.' 'When using weights, each bone affecting a vertex adds an additional vertex transform. For example, a mesh with 100 vertices requires 100 vertex transforms. If the same mesh has 2 bones affecting every vertex, it requires 200 vertex transforms.' Mitigation: 'Use prune to remove unnecessary weights and limit the number of bones that can affect a vertex.'

implementation_variants.name: Hull shaping for fill-rate, not just deformation
implementation_variants.description: 'The mesh hull should exclude as much blank space as possible ... Pixels outside the hull are not drawn at all and do not count against the fill rate. This can improve performance for a game that is fill rate limited, especially for large images with a lot of blank space.' Caveat: 'If the mesh hull is used to cut off nontransparent pixels, the resulting edge will have aliasing ... To get smooth edges in this case, multisample anti-aliasing (MSAA) can be used.'

implementation_variants.name: Linked meshes for skin/asset reuse
implementation_variants.description: 'To create a linked mesh ... The linked mesh shares its mesh structure with the source mesh: vertices, edges, texture coordinates, and weights. Any changes made to these for the source mesh will also affect all its linked meshes.' Constraint: 'Linked meshes must always be under the same slot as the source mesh.'

implementation_variants.name: Unity 2D Animation: bones + auto geometry + auto weights + bone influence list
implementation_variants.description: Authoring order: 'create the bones of the actor skeleton, generate and edit its mesh geometry, and adjust the weights that bind the bones to the meshes'. 'It is recommended to use the Auto Geometry tool to auto-generate the geometry Mesh.' Critical precondition: 'The Auto Weights tool only generates weights for Sprites that have both a geometry Mesh, and bones intersecting their Mesh.' Per-sprite influence sets are edited explicitly in the 'Bone Influence' panel.

implementation_variants.name: Round-robin or shared-pose updates for crowds
implementation_variants.description: Documented CPU escape hatch: 'If you have many skeletons, it may be acceptable to only update a subset of them each frame, in a round-robin fashion. Another option may be to only animate a small number of skeletons and use those poses to render a larger number of skeletons.'

skeletal_2d_deform.applicability_conditions: Use when you need interpolation/blending between motions, reusable rigs across characters or skins, or runtime procedural motion - and when your art can be authored as separated parts with a mesh. Do not use when the art direction depends on per-frame hand-drawn silhouettes (the Cuphead case, 50,000 frames) or when the deformation needed is essentially free-form squash that weights cannot express. Also note the authoring precondition in Unity: no mesh or no intersecting bone means no auto weights, i.e. rigging fails silently rather than erroring.
skeletal_2d_deform.limitations: CPU-bound, not GPU-bound: 'Transforming a vertex uses the CPU', 'Computing a bone's world transform uses the CPU'. Fill rate is the second bottleneck and is made worse by deformation, because 'Completely transparent pixels still use up fill rate, so attachments should be hidden rather than their alpha set to zero'. Clipping is called out as 'very expensive'. Critically, the vendor refuses to give absolute limits: 'Performance relies on so many variables that it isn't possible to generalize about which numbers in the metrics view are too high ... you will need to perform your own tests using your actual skeletons'.
skeletal_2d_deform.required_data_and_tools: A rigging tool with weight painting (Spine, Unity 2D Animation Skinning Editor, DragonBones, Live2D); a metrics view that reports bones, vertex transforms, triangles, area and draw calls; an atlas packer (atlas packing is the draw-call lever, not geometry merging); and your own profiler, since no universal threshold is published.

impact.cpu: medium to high (vertex transforms + bone world transforms + constraints + timelines, all CPU-side; scales with on-screen skeleton count)
impact.gpu: low geometry cost; potentially high fill-rate cost through overdraw and transparent pixels
impact.ram: low (bone transforms and mesh data are small; the saving is in texture memory versus frame-by-frame art)
impact.vram: low to medium (atlased sprite pages; much smaller than the equivalent frame-by-frame sprite set)

skeletal_2d_deform.quality_impact: Trades per-frame authored expressiveness for blending, reusability and memory. The visible failure modes are weight-bleed at joints, mesh tearing at sparse vertex density, and MSAA-dependent aliasing when hulls cut non-transparent pixels.
skeletal_2d_deform.concept_impact: Makes 2D animation data-driven: new motions are transforms, not art, which is what makes procedural 2D animation, hit reactions and equipment/skin systems practical.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2d rigging standard (vertex budget, influence cap, naming) + 4d rig one representative character + 2d runtime integration and metrics instrumentation + 2d atlas/packing policy + 2d QA of joint deformation at extreme poses. p80 adds 18d for re-rigging assets authored before the standard, weight cleanup/prune passes, and building tooling to enforce the budget in the importer.

relations.note: In 2D skeletal animation the draw-call lever is the atlas, not the mesh: 'Usually a batch needs to be flushed when the GPU needs to draw from a different texture, so a texture atlas is used to reduce texture switches.'
Spine's round-robin subset update is a hand-rolled equivalent of an animation update-rate budget; the 3D engines ship it as a plugin (Animation Budget Allocator) and the 2D tool leaves it to you.
A hand-drawn frame-by-frame art direction is fundamentally incompatible with skeletal deformation; this is a concept-stage conflict, not a tuning problem.

Structurally the same problem (deform a mesh from a bone hierarchy) solved on the opposite processor: 2D tools deform on the CPU and re-upload, 3D engines deform on the GPU and cache. Choose by art style, not by performance folklore.

skeletal_2d_deform.verification: Read the tool's metrics view with the real scene loaded and record bones, vertex transforms, triangles and area; then drive CPU and fill rate to the limit separately - halve vertex counts to test the CPU hypothesis, and cut overdraw to test the fill-rate hypothesis - and only then decide which budget to enforce in the importer.
